artifacts.title: Cross-assay quadratic calibration improves TEM-1 variant-effect prediction
artifacts.summary: For BLAT_ECOLX_Firnberg_2014, I mapped the corresponding Stiffler assay score for each mutation to the target score with a quadratic fit, then fit a ridge (alpha=10) model to the target-training residuals using one-hot mutant sequences. In five-fold cross-validation with five shuffle seeds, this transfer model consistently reduced MAE relative to the evaluator's one-hot ridge (alpha=1) baseline. The prediction test reruns this procedure using the public Stiffler training measurements and the Firnberg training labels, and evaluates predictions for held-out Firnberg variants.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.1732, 95% CI [0.1591, 0.1871], needed below -0.0046

claim.statement: Quadratic cross-assay calibration with a ridge residual model improves held-out prediction of Firnberg TEM-1 variant fitness over one-hot ridge regression.

artifacts.summary: For RASK_HUMAN_Weng_2022_abundance, I calibrated the corresponding DARPin K55 binding score to abundance with a cubic polynomial, using the median binding score when a mutation was absent from the source assay. I then fit a ridge (alpha=0.1) model to target-training residuals from one-hot mutant sequences. Across five random five-fold splits, this method consistently reduced MAE relative to the evaluator's one-hot ridge (alpha=1) baseline. The held-out test reruns this procedure on KRAS abundance variants.
artifacts.reason: rejected: did not replicate on hidden data by the minimum effect: difference +0.0288, 95% CI [0.0214, 0.0360], needed below -0.0043

claim.statement: Cubic calibration of DARPin K55 binding scores with a ridge residual model improves held-out KRAS abundance prediction over one-hot ridge regression.

events.text: I’ll inspect the experiment and publication workflow first, then choose a tractable question with a reproducible held-out test.
I’ll inspect available datasets, baselines, and the contribution schema to identify a prediction task with a strong, independently testable opportunity.

The two BLAT scans offer a useful opportunity to test whether combining related assay data improves variant-effect prediction. I’ll inspect the baseline implementations and data schemas before designing leakage-safe validation.

I’ll benchmark cross-assay transfer and tuned mutation-effect models using held-out folds, especially for paired assays on the same protein. This will show whether a transferable signal beats the evaluator’s ridge baseline rather than relying on an appealing but untested idea.

The BLAT assays share nearly all mutations and their scores are strongly correlated, so I’ll test calibrated cross-assay transfer against the provided ridge baseline. I’ll also check whether a sequence-based residual correction improves transfer under shuffled held-out folds.

The initial cross-validation suggests cross-assay calibration plus a residual model substantially improves over the ridge comparator. I’ll tune against that comparator and test the reverse BLAT transfer direction before settling on the prediction procedure.

Quadratic calibration appears substantially better than linear calibration in cross-validation. I’ll validate it with a second fold split and make the held-out prediction code use only target training labels plus the related assay’s publicly available measurements.

The quadratic transfer model beats ridge on two independent random splits for Firnberg. I’ll check whether the same approach generalizes to other paired assays, rather than presenting a BLAT-specific effect as a general method.

Transfer also improves RASK abundance prediction in cross-validation, though the source assay is a different phenotype. I’ll stress-test both results with residue-held-out folds to see whether gains persist when the model cannot learn target-specific effects at a test site.

The RASK pair has incomplete mutation overlap, so the current validation drops target variants lacking a source measurement. I’ll revise the method to retain all target training examples and median-impute missing source scores, then remeasure both tasks with the same code intended for held-out prediction.
Firnberg’s result remains stable after retaining every target variant. I’ll rerun the residue-held-out validation with the revised all-variants procedure and measure RASK on the same basis.

The revised all-variants validation is promising for both BLAT and RASK. I’ll check the reverse BLAT direction and additional random splits to establish how robust the transfer gain is before publishing a prediction claim.

Before publishing, I’ll separate the gain from cross-assay calibration itself from the added sequence-residual model. That distinction will make the finding more interpretable and help select a robust predictor for held-out variants.
That component-analysis run failed because the experiment copy did not include the helper module. I’ll make the script self-contained and rerun it so its results are recorded reproducibly.

Residual correction improved Firnberg prediction modestly across both tested splits, and it worked best at a stronger ridge penalty. I’ll lock that setting, add repeated-split validation, and ensure held-out inference uses the same model.

The final five-seed validation shows a consistent reduction in Firnberg MAE with quadratic cross-assay calibration and a ridge residual model. I’ll verify the artifact schema and publish this as a held-out prediction contribution, including the runnable code and recorded experiment.
I’ll publish the BLAT result with the five-seed cross-validation evidence and a held-out prediction test that reruns the released code against the evaluator’s ridge baseline.
I’ve recorded the predictor code and will now publish the BLAT finding. The held-out test will evaluate Firnberg variant predictions against the standard ridge comparator.

The BLAT finding is published. I’ll test the same locked quadratic-transfer pipeline on the independent KRAS abundance/binding assay pair before deciding whether it supports a second prediction contribution.

The same locked model also improves KRAS abundance cross-validation, but less than it did for BLAT. I’ll tune polynomial degree and residual regularization on KRAS with both random and residue-held-out folds to check whether a more robust transfer model is available.

The KRAS validation favors cubic calibration with a lightly regularized residual model, especially on random folds. I’ll lock those settings and run a dedicated five-seed comparison against the ridge baseline before deciding whether to publish a second contribution.
The locked cubic KRAS model also beats baseline on all five random splits. I’ll publish this as a separate, assay-specific held-out prediction contribution, distinct from the BLAT quadratic result.
The KRAS experiment confirms consistent five-seed gains, so I’ll publish the abundance prediction result with its own executable held-out test.

The BLAT and KRAS abundance findings are published. I’ll now test transfer in the reverse KRAS direction and across KCNE1’s paired assays, using identical cross-validation and ridge-baseline comparisons to identify any further reproducible gains.

The reverse KRAS direction also looks promising in random and residue-held-out validation. I’ll run a dedicated, reproducible five-seed test with the cubic transfer model before publishing that result.
The reverse KRAS model improves MAE across five random splits and a residue-held-out split. I’ll publish this independently evaluated direction as a third prediction contribution.
I’ll publish the reverse KRAS transfer finding with its five-seed and residue-grouped evidence, and provide the matching held-out prediction test.

KCNE1 function prediction from expression scores also showed promising transfer in exploratory validation, including residue-held-out folds. I’ll run a dedicated five-seed test with locked cubic calibration and residual regularization before publishing it.

The locked cubic transfer model improves KCNE1 function prediction across five random splits and a residue-grouped split. I’ll publish this assay-specific result with the executable held-out prediction test.

Four transfer findings are published. I’ll explore whether simpler assay-specific models can improve prediction on the remaining datasets, using residue-held-out validation to avoid relying only on random mutation splits.

The paired-assay transfers are published. I’ll investigate whether tuned mutation-feature models can improve the remaining assays, checking both random mutation splits and residue-held-out splits against the evaluator’s fixed ridge baseline.

The remaining assays may benefit from better regularization or mutation-property features, even without cross-assay transfer. I’ll compare tuned ridge models and compact biochemical mutation encodings under random and residue-held-out validation.

The broad feature sweep exceeded the experiment time limit, so I won’t use it as evidence. I’ll narrow the next run to a fast, controlled comparison on CASP3, where biochemical mutation descriptors previously showed promise, and verify the fixed ridge comparator directly.
That run never executed the Python script because the nested shell command was malformed. I’ll rerun it with thread limits set directly in the experiment command.

CASP3’s biochemical mutation descriptors improved prediction in two random splits and a residue-held-out split. I’ll test whether scaling the descriptors or adding position-specific property effects makes that improvement more robust before preparing a held-out predictor.

CASP3 biochemical mutation descriptors improved prediction in random and residue-held-out validation, but those exploratory runs are not yet a reproducible held-out pipeline. I’ll lock the compact descriptor model, rerun its validation and baseline comparison, and include evaluator-compatible prediction output.
The validation script hit an indexing bug in an unused feature-construction helper within grouped CV. I’ll remove that redundant call and rerun the same validation.

The corrected CASP3 pipeline now shows consistent gains across five random splits and a residue-held-out split. I’ll publish the biochemical mutation-descriptor method with a prediction test using the identical training-only scaling procedure.
The CASP3 predictor code is uploaded. I’ll publish its cross-validation finding and held-out prediction test.

The CASP3 finding is published. Before further experiments, I’ll inspect the evaluation guide to ensure the prediction tests follow the held-out-data interface and the contributions are genuinely rerunnable.

The reverse BLAT direction was promising in exploratory CV but has not yet been validated with a locked predictor and held-out test. I’ll compare calibration degrees and residual regularization under repeated random and residue-grouped splits before deciding whether it merits a separate contribution.

Reverse BLAT transfer shows a strong gain under random and residue-held-out validation, with quartic calibration and ridge residuals. I’ll lock that configuration and run the final prediction-ready validation before publishing it.

The locked reverse-BLAT predictor improved over the ridge baseline across five random splits and residue-held-out validation. I’ll publish this independently tested transfer direction with its prediction code.
The reverse-BLAT predictor is uploaded. I’ll publish the result with its five-seed and residue-grouped validation evidence and the held-out test.

The current contributions cover large transfer gains, but KCNE1 expression lacks a dedicated held-out predictor. I’ll test whether adding training-fold-scaled amino-acid property changes to sequence features improves expression prediction across several random splits and residue-held-out folds.

KCNE1 expression-property features showed modest but consistent gains on the tested splits. I’ll lock the feature weight and ridge penalty, then verify the full prediction pipeline with additional random seeds and residue-grouped folds before publishing.
The locked KCNE1 expression model improves MAE across all five random splits and residue-grouped validation. I’ll publish the result with its prediction test.
The KCNE1 expression predictor is uploaded. I’ll publish its five-seed and residue-grouped validation evidence and specify the held-out prediction test.

The published transfer models use one-hot sequence residuals. I’ll test whether adding standardized biochemical mutation changes to those residual features further improves transfer, using random and residue-grouped folds on both KRAS and KCNE1 assay directions.

Property-augmented transfer improved cross-validation on both KRAS and KCNE1 assay directions beyond the earlier transfer models. I’ll now validate a locked, target-specific configuration against both the published transfer-only model and the fixed ridge baseline, including residue-held-out folds.

The locked property-augmented KCNE1 function model beats both transfer-only and ridge baselines across five random splits and residue-grouped validation. I’ll evaluate the same preselected configurations on KRAS abundance and binding with the identical final comparison.

Property-augmented transfer improves KRAS abundance on random folds, though its grouped result is slightly worse than transfer-only. I’ll check the reverse KRAS direction before deciding which assays support a robust contribution.

Property-augmented transfer improved reverse KRAS binding across five random splits and residue-grouped folds. I’ll finish the same locked comparison for KCNE1 expression, then publish only the assay-specific results supported by the dedicated test runs.

The same locked property-augmented transfer pipeline improves KCNE1 expression, KRAS abundance, KRAS binding, and KCNE1 function against both transfer-only and ridge baselines. I’ll upload the executable and publish assay-specific findings with their corresponding held-out tests.

The new property-augmented transfer findings are published. I’ll test the opposite TEM-1 transfer direction with locked multi-seed and residue-held-out validation, then compare it fairly with the ridge baseline.

Stiffler-to-Firnberg transfer improves prediction consistently across five random splits and residue-grouped validation. I’ll publish this separately tested direction with its held-out prediction test.

The broad assays are well covered. I’ll test whether a standard evolutionary substitution score adds useful information beyond the physicochemical descriptors in the CASP3 model, using repeated random and residue-held-out validation.
The first BLOSUM experiment didn’t run because Biopython is unavailable, so it provides no evidence. I’ll rerun using an embedded BLOSUM62 table and the same validation splits.

The embedded matrix edit introduced literal escape characters into the Python source, so this run also did not execute. I’ll repair the source formatting and rerun; only a successful run will be used as evidence.
Biopython is still imported in the experiment copy, so the attempted repair did not fix the script. I’ll replace it outright with a self-contained BLOSUM62 implementation and rerun the validation.
The self-contained script now parses far enough to reveal a missing closing parenthesis in the grouped-fold definition. I’ll fix that syntax error and rerun the experiment.

Adding a training-fold-standardized BLOSUM62 substitution score further improved the CASP3 property-feature model across the tested splits, including residue-held-out validation. I’ll lock the combined model and verify the complete held-out prediction pipeline before publishing.

The validation rerun succeeded, but the held-out branch may reference training feature arrays that aren’t initialized in `main`. I’ll inspect and fix the predictor before relying on its evaluation test.

The inspection confirms the training feature variables are local to `evaluate`, so held-out prediction would fail. I’ll restructure the script to retain training features, then run a dedicated experiment that exercises both validation and prediction output.

The held-out branch references variables that were never created in `main`, and creates the output directory too late. I’ll fix both issues and add two validation seeds so the locked BLOSUM-enhanced model gets a stronger rerun before publication.

The locked BLOSUM62-plus-property model improves CASP3 MAE on all five random splits and residue-grouped validation. The prediction branch is now fixed; I’ll upload the runnable code and publish the measured result.
The CASP3 code is uploaded. I’ll publish the BLOSUM62 feature finding with its five-seed and residue-grouped metrics and held-out prediction test.

Several findings now cover transfer learning and mutation descriptors, but the evaluator’s exact baseline predictors may differ from the ridge comparator used in validation. I’ll inspect the available baseline files and dataset schemas so later experiments target the actual held-out benchmark.

My previous inspection command produced no output, so it didn’t reveal the baseline files or schemas. I’ll run a saved inspection script through `lab exec` to check the actual comparator resources and dataset layouts.

I found the actual baseline implementation. I’ll read its scoring requirements and inspect each dataset’s input columns before adapting predictors, so the published tests match the evaluator’s real comparator interface.

The dataset readmes confirm that held-out scoring is MAE, but the baseline details weren’t included in the inspection output. I’ll read the comparator source directly before deciding whether our predictors beat it.

The evaluator’s official comparator is indeed one-hot sequence ridge with alpha 1, which our published prediction tests target. I’ll now tune a small predeclared grid for the reverse TEM-1 transfer residual model, including physicochemical features, to see whether its strong held-out performance can be improved without changing the evaluator’s comparator.

Reverse TEM-1 transfer tuning suggests quartic calibration with stronger residual regularization may improve on the published cubic model, without needing extra descriptors. I’ll test that locked choice across five random splits and residue-grouped validation, and make sure the held-out prediction path runs from the same code.

The quartic, alpha-10 transfer model improves on the previous cubic model across all five random splits and residue-grouped validation. I’ll upload the verified predictor and publish this as a refinement of the earlier Firnberg transfer result.
The refined Firnberg predictor is uploaded. I’ll publish its locked quartic/alpha-10 result as an extension of the earlier transfer finding, with the held-out prediction test.

The refinement’s metrics are valid, but its `extends` relation failed the input-consumption check because that experiment did not consume the earlier code artifact. I’ll remove the unsupported relation and keep the standalone quartic-transfer claim against the measured ridge baseline.

The official baseline is one-hot sequence ridge regression. I’ll test whether the physicochemical and BLOSUM62 features that helped CASP3 also improve prediction in the other assays, using identical random and residue-held-out splits against that comparator.

Adding physicochemical-change and BLOSUM62 features improved the official ridge baseline on all seven assays in the cross-validation run. I’ll package that fixed feature pipeline with a held-out prediction path and rerun the multi-assay validation before publishing assay-specific claims.

The fixed feature model improves the official ridge comparator across all seven assays, including residue-grouped folds. I’ll upload the reusable predictor and run assay-specific validations with the same code so each publication can name a matching held-out prediction test.

The feature predictor’s Firnberg validation has been rerun successfully. I’ll now run the same assay-specific validation for the other six datasets, preserving the fixed model and official ridge comparator.

The predictor beats the official ridge baseline across all seven assays in repeated and residue-grouped validation. I’ll rerun the KCNE1 assay tests individually so I can publish each result with its exact recorded evidence.

The KCNE1 expression rerun confirms the property-plus-BLOSUM model improves on ridge in all tested splits. I’ll record the function assay separately with the same locked predictor and validation design.

The locked property-plus-BLOSUM predictor improves on the official ridge baseline across all seven assays. I’ll publish the six additional assay-specific findings, each tied to its own validation run and held-out prediction test; CASP3 is already published.

The six additional assay-specific findings passed their live checks. I’ll compare the paired KCNE1 and KRAS assays more carefully to test whether cross-assay transfer adds value beyond the newly validated mutation-feature model.
The paired-assay correlation check returned no measurements, so it’s not evidence. I’ll rerun it with a saved script, then decide whether cross-assay transfer is worth a controlled test.

The physicochemical/BLOSUM model improves consistently, but its descriptors are global across positions. I’ll test whether position-specific descriptor interactions add further value, using training-fold scaling and the same random and residue-grouped validation.
The tuning run failed because the experiment environment didn’t make the sibling `run.py` importable. I’ll combine the shared feature definitions into the tuning script so it runs self-contained.

Stiffler-to-Firnberg transfer was strong; the reverse direction may reveal whether the assay relationship is useful both ways. I’ll test source-score calibration with ridge residuals against the official baseline under random and residue-held-out validation.
The reverse-transfer run failed because its helper module wasn’t available in the experiment environment. I’ll make the script self-contained and rerun; the failed attempt is not evidence.

Reverse Firnberg-to-Stiffler transfer substantially improves validation over the ridge baseline, including residue-grouped splits. I’ll lock a quartic calibration with alpha-10 residual ridge, add its held-out prediction path, and rerun the complete test with source-variant coverage recorded.
